passage: Matter is composed of tiny, indivisible building blocks called atoms, which are not solid balls but contain vast amounts of empty space. When substances are heated, these atoms do not grow in size; instead, they simply move faster and spread further apart. Atoms combine in fixed, whole-number ratios to form compounds, and this ratio remains constant regardless of whether the substance is found in nature or synthesized in a laboratory. During chemical reactions, the total mass remains unchanged, even if a gas is produced, because atoms are merely rearranged rather than created or destroyed. A molecule is defined as the smallest particle of an element or a compound that can exist independently. While atoms can gain or lose electrons to form ions, they never change their identity by gaining or losing protons in the nucleus. Finally, the molar mass of a substance represents the mass of one mole of particles, which is a specific collection of 6.022 x 10^23 atoms or molecules, rather than the mass of a single atom or molecule in grams. Understanding these principles allows us to calculate chemical quantities accurately by dividing the given mass by the molar mass, rather than multiplying them.

items.evidence: When substances are heated, these atoms do not grow in size; instead, they simply move faster and spread further apart.
items.q: A copper rod is heated strongly. What happens to the copper atoms inside it?
options: They move quicker and drift further apart
They grow bigger and push the rod longer
They gain protons and become new atoms
They break into smaller pieces of matter
items.explain: Heating does not make atoms bigger; atoms just move faster and spread further apart.

wrong.why: thinks atoms grow in size when heated
thinks atoms can gain protons and change

items.evidence: During chemical reactions, the total mass remains unchanged, even if a gas is produced, because atoms are merely rearranged rather than created or destroyed.
items.q: Marble reacts with acid in a sealed flask and bubbles of gas form. What happens to the total mass?
options: It stays the same as at the start
It falls because the gas escapes into bubbles
It rises because new atoms are created
It depends on how the acid was made
items.explain: Atoms are only rearranged, not created or destroyed, so total mass stays the same even when gas forms.

wrong.why: thinks producing a gas means mass is lost
thinks preparation method changes the result

items.evidence: Atoms combine in fixed, whole-number ratios to form compounds, and this ratio remains constant regardless of whether the substance is found in nature or synthesized in a laboratory.
items.q: Pure water from a river is compared with pure water made in a lab. How do their atom ratios compare?
options: They are exactly equal in both samples
They differ because the lab chose its own ratio
They differ because nature mixes atoms randomly
They differ because the lab atoms were heated
items.explain: A compound always has the same fixed ratio of atoms, whether from nature or a laboratory.

wrong.why: thinks preparation method decides the ratio
thinks natural compounds have no fixed ratio
thinks heating changes the atoms themselves

items.evidence: Understanding these principles allows us to calculate chemical quantities accurately by dividing the given mass by the molar mass, rather than multiplying them.
items.q: Water's molar mass is 18 g. How should Asha find the moles in 36 g of water?
items.explain: Moles are found by dividing the given mass by the molar mass: 36 ÷ 18 = 2 moles.

wrong.why: thinks molar mass is one molecule's mass
